speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, besides rising prices, rising interest rates will impact Singaporeans and their cash or payment outlays.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The US Federal Reserve System (the Fed) officials have indicated that interest rates may continue to rise and hit close to 4.6% in 2023.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some market participants are even forecasting it to reach 5%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, there are no stated upper limits to what the Fed can hike rates to, to achieve their inflation mandate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recent market volatility has also led to higher cost of funds and interest rates and we are not immune to these sharp moves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like me, many Members of this House have raised Parliamentary Questions or otherwise spoken about these issues in the last few months, both on rising prices and on rising interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Motion today is specifically on rising interest rates, what it means for Singapore and how we can help Singaporeans in this environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In line with the Government's approach in recent times, I believe there is room for targeted interventions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For this Motion, I want to focus on helping Singaporeans transition from a low interest rate environment to a high interest rate environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The world is unlikely to return anytime soon to the low inflation levels and interest rates it has enjoyed in recent decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am also heartened by recent Department of Statistics data and expert assessments that households will be able to weather higher interest rates and a potential economic recession given their financial positions as at the 2nd quarter of 2022, as their household assets-to-liabilities ratio remains healthy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nonetheless, if interest rates rise significantly higher, one might wonder whether the expected assumptions behind these assessments will remain valid.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, in the short-term, we can and should help Singaporeans make the transition to this new normal or new "abnormal" of high interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many Singaporean families have existing borrowings to finance big-ticket items like their mortgages, cars and education, and many of them have carefully budgeted, saved and invested to achieve their financial objectives, although based on the old normal.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that the Government is in the midst of formulating measures to help Singaporeans cope with the upcoming economic headwinds and would like to provide some suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first suggestion: more can be done in filling the information gap on higher interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure that many Singaporeans, like me, have received notices from their banks that their loan rates are going up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The notices are quite brief, stating not much more beyond the new rate percentage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That may not be helpful to less financially savvy Singaporeans, who might not realise how they might be impacted by that increase, including how much more income or savings they would need to service the loan subsequently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have had residents emailing to meet me physically, to share with me their financial issues with servicing loans, where I realised that they did not understand that their payments paid off the interest first and the principal later.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this sort of backdrop, we must ensure that the banks and other institutions that provide loans of all kinds, including the non-bank financial institutions and authorised money lenders and so on, proactively clarify the impact to their borrowers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there are various mortgage loan calculators offered by some banks and other websites on the Internet, not everyone may know of them or how to use them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One simple solution would be to shift this task to the banks, financial and other lending institutions, who are sophisticated enough to model the practical effects relatively easily.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there may be certain uncertainties that may affect the precise impact of an interest rate rise on a particular borrower, the financial institutions can provide an indicative range to give the borrower an idea.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This boils down to the basic principle of balancing caveat emptor for the investor/customer versus whether banks owe a social duty of care to more than just the average bank customer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of the less sophisticated retail investors and retail bank customers might not have the same level of savviness as the "average median investor".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This should not be unfamiliar to the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Insurance agents are already required to provide the benefits illustration in an endowment policy proposal based on different scenarios of investment rates of return.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Financial institutions offering credit cards or mortgages are required by MAS to provide projections of instalment payments under different scenarios.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are all similarly aimed at giving the end-consumer an easy-to-understand picture of the financial calculations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will also mean that the financial institutions may be able to pre-empt when homebuyers might encounter issues servicing higher home loans if their incomes and savings rates have become insufficient.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In such cases, I hope the Government or relevant agencies work with the financial institutions to allow for longer-term mortgage tenures to accommodate homebuyers who struggle to pay higher instalments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or at the very least be more alert now about such cases and offer some flexibility in the current environment as a baseline.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second suggestion: we should enhance the flexibility of some of our policies, in order to support the more leveraged and vulnerable households that may require help amidst higher borrowing costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The fixed interest rate on HDB loans was certainly less attractive just months ago, when bank loan rates were as low as 1.15% to 1.5%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the present global interest rate hikes set to continue, they will now be locked into a higher rate than the HDB rate which they were trying to find a lower alternative for.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I understand that the policy is that homeowners who opt for, or refinance using bank loans can no longer take up a HDB loan, perhaps the HDB can consider allowing eligible households to make a one-time transfer back to HDB loans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I am mindful that it may have some backend implications for the banks, a refinancing sort of mechanism, if one is eligible, could be one possible approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The HDB loan rate is pegged at 0.1% above the prevailing Central Provident Fund (CPF) Ordinary Account (OA) interest rate, and HDB and CPF have recently confirmed that the applicable rates will remain unchanged until the end of this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that the standing policy is for the OA interest rate to be reviewed every three months.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the impact of changes in rates on borrowers' finances in the medium-term, it would be helpful if the Government or HDB is able to provide HDB borrowers more advanced guidance on potential rate changes, beyond three months.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will allow new and existing homeowners to make a more certain choice on how they finance their home, to better prepare them amidst this new normal of interest rate levels that we may be entering.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On balance, the information provided will help household decisions but the impact of the extent in which this becomes a de facto forward guidance on the rates will need to be considered in totality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also ensure that Singapore is prepared in the extraordinary event where home loan rates rise sharply, such as if the US Fed raises their rates to above 5%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The US mortgage rates have already hit 6% for the first time since 2008.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Government have any contingency plans in place?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will MAS consider implementing temporary measures, such as rate ceilings to ensure that rates do not spiral out of control and become unaffordable?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, there are already maximum annual percentage interest rates on credit card and pawn loans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many countries around the world, including our neighbours Indonesia and Malaysia, have forms of subsidised housing loans targeted at lower-income citizens, and this is also an interim policy measure that is worth considering for vulnerable groups not captured by the concessionary HDB loan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides housing, education is another key reason for Singaporeans' borrowing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There has always been a strong policy reason to ensure that our students who are trying to secure a good education are not saddled with heavy debt before they enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the Ministry of Education (MOE) Study Loan allows low-income households to obtain loans that are interest-free for a limited or entire duration of the loan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The CPF Education Loan Scheme allows for the use of one's CPF OA savings to pay for one's own, children's or spouse's tuition fees for full-time diploma or degree courses at approved educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will benefit a greater pool of Singaporeans who are in the pursuit of better education, better skills and who will ultimately be an asset in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Academic studies using US data have shown that an upskilled workforce has positive externalities to a sector, beyond the individual's gains.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My third suggestion: we should not stop at assistance for individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and firms, especially those that operate in sectors that are highly reliant on external financing, will require targeted help as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our economy plays catch-up from the time lost during the pandemic, there might be a need to take a targeted sector-specific approach in limiting the adverse effects that might be brought about by higher interest rates that we cannot avoid.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To prevent a hard landing from steep hikes in the cost of capital, our SMEs will need some support in transitioning to have enough reaction time to adjust their plans for cashflow, servicing existing debt and taking on new debt.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There might also be a need to take a targeted sector-specific approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Construction and manufacturing are sectors that are known to be sensitive to interest rate hikes as they are capital-intensive and dependent on commercial loans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will focus on construction firms as their cash flows are also tighter due to the longer-term nature of construction projects, which have not been helped by the labour and cost disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The construction sector is critical to renewing Singapore's physical infrastructure, which itself is a key driver of our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has already contributed to a tight housing supply situation and left many households in limbo waiting for their new houses to be completed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, any uncertainty in interest rates could throw the sector into disarray again, within this post-pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is important for the sector to be able to continue to access affordable loans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may not be commercially viable to expect commercial banks to cap or limit the interest rates charged to construction firms, especially when they have to price in the fact that the construction sector has already been trending towards a higher risk of defaulting on repayments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But aside from arguments about consolidation as a form of creative destruction in this sector and that some of the firms may have limited long-term viability anyway, the Government may need to step in to provide reliable and affordable sources of temporary financing to eligible SMEs and firms – temporary financing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I am thinking of schemes, such as the Temporary Bridging Loan Programme (TBLP) that was rolled out during the pandemic, as well as the Temporary Electricity Contracting Support Scheme (TRECS), which offer firms the ability to lock in a favourable interest rate or electricity tariff, at times where such rates are extremely volatile.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the sake of fiscal prudence, I do not mean that we should commit to subsidising firms for a prolonged duration.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What I have in mind is simply a temporary measure, to help our vulnerable firms and SMEs deal with interest rates that have doubled and may perhaps triple in just over a period of months.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I urge the Government to provide updates as soon as possible on the duration of any support measures to help our firms with their forward planning.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even as we try to enhance our long-term economic growth in this environment, we are fighting business decisions to reduce investments, made amidst higher hurdle rates for projects and investments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, in addition, can the Government work further with financial institutions to keep the processing fees of these Government-assisted loans as low as possible?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To add, we should make sure that the measures apply across both bank and non-bank financial institutions or lenders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The latter might rise in prominence in the lending sector, if the rise in interest rates makes it harder for those with relatively lower credit worthiness or urgent credit needs to access bank loans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My fourth and final suggestion on this front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we transition into a new high-interest rate environment, our metrics for measuring systemic risk may need to be adjusted as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our efforts to measure this improperly or with a decent lag can lead to social implications.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There have been numerous mentions of the Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR) in this House, in response to Members' concerns over the interest rate and debt situation in Singapore, in the last few months.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The TDSR framework captures a borrower's monthly expenses on all types of debt, including mortgages, car loans and unsecured debt as a proportion of income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Essentially, MAS sets a ceiling that only 55% of a borrower's income should be spent on servicing debt obligations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By lowering the ceiling, MAS can "tighten" the threshold up to which a person may borrow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The interest rate that is used to calculate loan repayments under the TDSR is the higher of 3.5% or the prevailing market rate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The idea was to build in a buffer against interest rate rises for borrowers who have taken out a mortgage in the past.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, with today's bank interest rates hitting more than 3% and the US Fed's expectation that its benchmark interest rate may hit close to 4.4% as soon as this year, and possibly some more next year, the "buffer" that is built into MAS' monitoring framework may soon be completely eroded.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, is this move sufficient to maintain the robustness of MAS monitoring and stress testing?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the rate of global interest rate increases and their potential landing points at up to 5%, is MAS prepared to raise this again, potentially in a matter of a few months?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, what is the impact of the current 0.5% adjustment on the TDSR data, and what would the projected impact of further increases be, considering the median TDSR of 43%?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I ask these questions because, in part, housing loans are a long tenure, with significant overhang and forward risk exposure if the interest rates go up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in an alternative worst-case scenario, if there is a wave of defaults/repossessions, there is always the risk of market instability with cascading social implications.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These interventions I have suggested above, Mr Speaker, would require the Government's use of its revenues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Global stocks and even cryptocurrencies have already taken a hit with the latest Fed announcements on the need for more interest rate hikes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Questions that probably need to be considered are first, what are the downside risks in the event of sell-offs in these holdings and what would be the impact on our fiscal position?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how may we also maximise the investment opportunities posed by a high interest rate environment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Minister or relevant agencies can shed some light on these questions as it has ramifications on our fiscal trajectory and outlook.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Government will take into consideration my suggestions above in positive light to mitigate the risk of higher interest rates on Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will need to take considered actions to put Singaporeans and our firms in good stead to adapt to and thrive in this situation, while the Government balances the fine line between keeping prices from rising further and dampening economic expansion in the post-COVID recovery period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our Government agencies will look into his points and his suggestions and I will respond to some of the key points that he raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Saktiandi observed, many central banks have been raising interest rates to tackle inflation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Similarly, MAS has taken steps to tighten monetary policy and is closely monitoring developments on this front.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is also alert to systemic risks to our financial system arising from higher interest rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will provide assistance to cushion the impact on households and businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is also important for all of us to take steps to adapt to this new environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I share Mr Saktiandi's view that the higher interest rates we are experiencing may not be a passing phenomenon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need to prepare ourselves for this change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For education, the Government currently subsidises over 90% of the costs of education from primary to pre-university level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The subsidy rate for Institute of Technical Education (ITE) is also more than 90%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For polytechnics and autonomous universities, Government subsidies amount to around 85% and 75% of total costs respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, students can apply for bursaries and education loans to support their education-related expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Tuition Fee Loan Scheme is available to all, while the Study Loan Scheme is available to students from lower- to middle-income households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Both loan schemes do not incur interest during study and require repayment only after graduation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are important support measures to ensure tertiary education remains affordable, and no Singaporean child will be denied of the opportunity to receive a good education because of financial difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On public housing, the Government will continue to sell new flats at prices below market value with significant housing subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The end in mind is to encourage home ownership, and to enable as many families as possible to own their homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister Desmond Lee spoke about this earlier today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the whole, the household debt situation in Singapore remains healthy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is because of our prudent policies on unsecured consumer lending and residential mortgages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Residential mortgages are subject to loan-to-value limits as well as debt servicing ratios, which cap the amount of debt and monthly mortgage payment individuals can take on when they purchase properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These will help ensure that property buyers continue to borrow prudently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to monitor the property market and review our polices where necessary in a rising interest rate environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also work with financial and non-financial institutions to better help borrowers understand their loan commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi highlighted the requirements MAS places on financial institutions to explain how a borrower's monthly mortgage instalments would vary if interest rates increased.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Non-financial institutions, such as licensed moneylenders (LMLs) are required to explain to the borrower the terms of the loan contract and the breakdown of each repayment that goes into servicing the principal amount and other costs, all in a language that the borrower understands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, LMLs are only permitted to impose fixed borrowing costs and fixed interest rates, ensuring that borrowers would not be caught off-guard by rising interest rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government provides assistance to businesses through various credit schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our economic agencies have assessed that there are available credit facilities for businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SME loan volumes, for example, have continued to be stable in recent months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With the expiry of the Temporary Bridging Loan Programme (TBLP), enterprises can still tap on the Enterprise Financing Scheme, which supports access to financing for a wide range of business activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our economic agencies will monitor the situation closely and review the need for further adjustments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Importantly, businesses would need to double down on efforts to improve productivity and upgrade the skills of their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will also continue to provide Workfare Income Supplement and other support measures to boost the earnings of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the near term, significant market uncertainties have resulted in a weaker investment environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The investment entities, such as the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) and Temasek, are closely monitoring macroeconomic and geopolitical developments, including changes to the interest rate environment, and they will continue to maintain diverse portfolios to manage investment risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we are able to benefit from this source of revenue today, and also during the COVID-19 pandemic, because previous generations of Singaporeans worked hard and built up our reserves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must likewise do the responsible thing by safeguarding our reserves and growing it further, so that we leave behind a strategic asset and lay the foundations for a better future that will benefit our children and grandchildren.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another important area is how all of us can play a role in helping one another in a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A key enabler is the high degree of trust in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Trust has allowed us to weather many uncertainties together, including our fight against COVID-19, and it will be a critical success factor as we face new challenges going ahead, such as rising inflation and higher interest rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like other Members of this House, I have come across many heartwarming examples of institutions, community organisations and also individual Singaporeans pitching in to help others who are facing difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They generously provide extra assistance to complement what the Government is giving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and I are both serving in Bishan-Toa Payoh GRC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we are grateful to our corporate and community partners who work with us to provide additional local-level assistance to our residents, especially the vulnerable and lower-income families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, my volunteers and I have been distributing monthly WeCare Packs containing food items and daily necessities to our lower-income families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I have also raised additional amounts through our community welfare fund to provide National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) vouchers and angbaos to our vulnerable residents —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, you have about 50 seconds left.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I know many Grassroots Advisers are doing the same, including Mr Saktiandi Supaat.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As we say at the Chinese Development Assistance Council (CDAC), 一人一点心，社会更温馨 .
